description: MedSpace AI is a solo team combining clinical medicine, biomedical research, and artificial intelligence. Led by a physician with experience in medical data analysis and machine learning, the team aims to develop practical, data-driven solutions for astronaut health monitoring and space exploration.
summary:
MedSpace AI is a web prototype that helps astronauts monitor physical symptoms and emotional well-being during long-duration missions. Crew members can describe concerns in their own words, record measurements, track trends, and choose which journal entries to keep private or include in an expert handoff.

The prototype organizes each check-in into a SOAP summary of reported concerns, recorded indicators, preliminary findings, and next steps. The public demo uses synthetic data, explainable rules, and photo previews. In local testing, a vision-language model described visible features in a synthetic health photo. Those observations can inform the local assessment alongside the crew member’s report and measurements.

During a simulated communications outage, crew members can queue a summary for expert review when the Earth link returns. Explicit statements of intent to harm someone trigger immediate onboard guidance. NASA Human Research Program resources informed the monitoring categories and the design for delayed communication. The prototype helps crew members recognize changes and gives Earth-based reviewers a timeline to assess.
details:
MedSpace AI is a browser-based prototype for tracking physical symptoms and emotional well-being during long-duration missions. A crew member can describe a concern in their own words, add available measurements, attach a health photo, and review trends across mission days. They can revisit earlier check-ins and download a structured report.

The prototype organizes each check-in into a SOAP summary: reported concerns, reference data, preliminary assessment, and next steps. The public website uses synthetic data, rule-based screening, and photo previews. In a separate local test, I used Ollama to run Qwen2.5 0.5B for text analysis and Qwen2.5-VL 3B for photo analysis. The vision model identified visible redness in a synthetic skin photo, although it misidentified the area of the arm. The app can use that observation alongside the crew member’s report and measurements when generating a preliminary assessment and next steps. If the model cannot produce usable guidance, the interface directs the crew member to their crew medical officer.

MedSpace AI simulates a communications gap with Earth. While offline, the crew member can queue a check-in for review. Simulated reconnection moves the queued summary to an expert review state. A separate onboard safety rule responds immediately to supported explicit statements about harming someone, even while model analysis is pending.

I designed the interface to make daily reporting easier while giving crew members control over sensitive material. For each journal entry or draft message, they can choose to keep it private, allow on-device analysis, or include it in the simulated Earth handoff. They can also choose whether a health photo stays on the device or accompanies the handoff as a reduced-size copy. A separate “Photos from home” album stays visible during the check-in and serves as a personal space.

I built the prototype with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using browser storage for local records, Canvas for trend charts, and Node.js for the local server and automated tests. ChatGPT/Codex assisted with development, debugging, testing, and writing. NASA Human Research Program resources on human spaceflight hazards and risks informed the monitoring categories and the design for delayed Earth review. The goal is to help crew members document changes promptly and give medical reviewers a clearer timeline when contact resumes.

The demo’s English narration was generated using Microsoft Zira text-to-speech.
